notes: \cpara{Names the most critical mistake: not realizing that solving a mystery should make it feel less confusing. As a warning sign the rule works in one direction. It catches an answer that leaves the mystery feeling mysterious, but not an answer that feels like an explanation and is not, the error ``Say Not Complexity'' describes: ``a causal node that feels like an explanation but isn't.''}
\cpara{Says the young author knew the standard histories but thought this mystery was new and harder.}
\cpara{Answers the young self: stars, matter and life were mysteries for thousands of years until science explained them.}
\cpara{A general claim about how ``the children of that generation'' greet each new puzzle, offered without evidence. The one case is the author's own.}
\cpara{Gives the young author's reading of history: the old mystics had a character flaw, and a truly weird phenomenon might deserve a weird explanation.}

\cpara{Says the author saw only later how reasonable vitalism had seemed at the time. The history is not told here; the post relies on ``Mysterious Answers to Mysterious Questions'' (25 August 2007), which quotes Lord Kelvin as a vitalist.}

\cpara{The claim is that living through those refutations would have prevented the mistake. The author's own example of a vitalist sits uneasily with it, though the theory Kelvin gave up was not a mysterious answer. Lord Kelvin, quoted in ``Mysterious Answers to Mysterious Questions,'' lived through a scientific revolution in his own field: he gave up Carnot's theory of heat for Joule's and helped formulate the laws of thermodynamics (Wikipedia, ``Lord Kelvin''). In the passage the author quotes, he still held it ``most probable that the animal body does not act as a thermodynamic engine,'' and the influence of life to be ``infinitely beyond the range of any scientific inquiry hitherto entered on.''}
